hook: You know this as the wedding reading. But did you know Paul wrote it to a church that was splitting into parties and suing each other?
story:
Read aloud at a wedding, “Love is patient and is kind” sounds like a promise between two people at an altar. Paul was not picturing a wedding. He was writing to a church that was coming apart.

He was writing from Ephesus, and word had come to him from Chloe’s household: “there are contentions among you.” Each member, he wrote, was saying “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos,” “I follow Cephas,” and, “I follow Christ.” Believers were taking one another to court. At the church’s shared meal, “One is hungry, and another is drunken.” And the people who had been given remarkable gifts, speaking in other languages, prophesying, were reveling in them.

That is the ground under this verse. Chapter 12 ends with Paul saying, “I show a most excellent way to you.” Chapter 13 opens with the gifts the Corinthians prized, and tells them that without love even the most dazzling of them is “a clanging cymbal.” Only then comes the list: patient, kind, not envious, not bragging, not seeking its own way. Chapter 14 begins, “Follow after love”

So the most quoted description of love in the Bible was first a mirror held up to a quarrelsome church by a man who still called them his brothers.

voices.name: Gordon Fee
voices.about: New Testament scholar, on what Paul had in mind
voices.words: Paul probably never considered a marriage ceremony or vow of romantic love when he penned the now-famous words in 1 Corinthians 13.

source.title: Gordon Fee, First Corinthians’ Love Passage (Bible Odyssey, Society of Biblical Literature)

moment:
Paul knew these people. He had come to Corinth earlier and stayed for a year and six months, and “Many of the Corinthians, when they heard, believed and were baptized.” They were not strangers he was lecturing from a distance.

The church was not a failure. Edward Adams, a New Testament scholar, notes that for all its troubles the church was a large congregation with lively worship. Gordon Fee reads the chapter as Paul’s hope for exactly this church: that it could change if its members chose the path of love.

That is why the list in verses 4 to 7 is so concrete. It does not say love is a warm feeling. It says what love does and does not do: it waits, it is kind, it does not envy, it does not brag, it does not push for its own way, it is not provoked. Set beside a church of rival parties, a table where some went hungry, and a stage for impressive gifts, each line lands somewhere.
around:
Just before the passage, Paul lists the gifts of the assembly and asks, “Are all apostles? Are all prophets?” Just after it, he says that prophecies and languages will end, and “For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face.” The chapter closes with faith, hope and love, and the verdict: “The greatest of these is love.”

Verses 4 to 7 are the middle of a short chapter that begins with gifts that are worth nothing without love, and ends with a love that outlasts every gift.
after:
Paul’s own time with this church did not end quietly. In a later letter to them he wrote that he had written to them “out of much affliction and anguish of heart” and “with many tears,” so that they might know the love he had for them. He does not say which letter he means. And in the same later letter he reports that news of them reached him through Titus, “your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.”

The quarrels did not stay in the first century. A letter that tradition ascribes to Clement, sent from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth during a later outbreak of discord, tells them to take up Paul’s epistle and describes love in words that could have been aimed at the old quarrel: love, it says, makes no schisms and gives rise to no seditions, and does all things in harmony.

In 1884, at a country house in England, the evangelist Dwight L. Moody asked a guest, Henry Drummond, to speak on Scripture. Drummond opened his small Testament to this chapter and spoke on love. Moody wrote that he would not rest until he had brought Drummond to his school at Northfield to give that address. In his introduction to the printed address he wrote that the one great need in the Christian life is more love to God and to each other, and he wished that everyone could move into that chapter and live there.
readings:
One reading hears the passage as the portrait of love in the closest human bond, which is why it is chosen for weddings, and why many couples with no connection to the church choose it too.

A second reading keeps it in the church where it was written. On this reading, Paul’s subject is how believers treat each other in the daily life of the assembly and with those outside, and the passage describes what love does when others come first.

A third, older habit of reading treats the list as a single thing seen in parts. The Scottish teacher Henry Drummond, in the address Moody heard in 1884, pictured Paul passing love through a crystal prism, so that it comes out as a spectrum of its parts: ordinary virtues that anyone can practice in any place in life.
argued: Do these words belong at a wedding? Two writers on Bible Odyssey, a site of the Society of Biblical Literature, answer differently. Gordon Fee writes: [[fee]] Christopher Skinner, who agrees that the church is the setting, still concludes the opposite about the wedding: [[skinner]] Both read the passage in its place first. They differ on whether it can be carried from there to a marriage.
point: These four verses were written for a divided church and a crowd of competing gifts. They describe love as something done: patience, kindness, putting others first. Read after the quarrels of Corinth, they are less a greeting card and more a very practical standard.
lesson:
You may know this passage by heart and still find it hard to read straight. It is not asking whether you feel loving. It is asking what you do when someone is slow, when someone gets the credit, when you are right and the other person is not.

Paul wrote it to people who were proud of their gifts and divided over their leaders. If you see yourself in that, you are in good company. Paul does not stop at their failure. He points them to a better road, and he points you to it too.

You might read the whole chapter today instead of only the middle, and choose one line to try in an ordinary place: at home, at work, in a conversation you would rather win. And if you do not share this faith, the list still says something that many people of any belief recognize: a love that is patient and kind, and does not keep a record of wrongs, is rare and worth wanting.

echoes.note: John gives the root of that kind of love: “We love him, because he first loved us.” In the Bible, love is first received, then practiced.
Paul tells another church, after listing patience and forgiveness: “Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.” Again love is what holds a community together.
Jesus says, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” He makes love among believers the sign that others can see.
